subject: pathology
title: Oedema, hyperaemia, congestion and haemorrhage

steps.tx: **Oedema** is excess interstitial fluid in tissues. Fluid movement follows Starling forces: **hydrostatic pressure** pushes fluid out of capillaries, while **oncotic pressure** from plasma albumin pulls it back in. Oedema arises when outward forces rise or inward forces fall. Only about 5 percent of body water sits in plasma, so small shifts matter.

steps.tx: **Hyperaemia** is an active increase in blood volume caused by arteriolar dilatation and greater inflow. **Congestion** is passive: blood backs up because venous outflow is impaired. Congestion is the key pathway in heart failure, where back pressure spreads to the lungs, liver, spleen and kidneys.

steps.tx: Chronic passive congestion of the **liver** produces a nutmeg liver. Right-sided failure, tricuspid regurgitation, constrictive pericarditis and mitral stenosis are common causes. Centrilobular zone 3 becomes congested and haemorrhagic, with necrosis. In chronic cases, fibrous bands link central veins to portal tracts, a pattern called cardiac sclerosis, which differs from bridging fibrosis.

steps.tx: **Heart failure cells** are hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages. In left-sided failure, raised pulmonary capillary pressure leaks red cells into alveoli. Macrophages digest them and store iron as hemosiderin. Their presence on bronchoalveolar lavage points to chronic pulmonary congestion. Iron stains blue with Prussian blue, and the lung is the most common extracardiac organ affected by left ventricular failure.

steps.tx: **Haemostasis** has three parts: endothelium, platelets and the coagulation system. Vascular injury first causes brief vasoconstriction. Platelets then adhere and aggregate to form a plug. Endothelial cells promote clotting through tissue factor and von Willebrand factor, while thrombomodulin and prostacyclin act as anticoagulants. Fibrinolysis, not vasospasm, is the later limiting step.
